messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ezekiel, a 68-year-old widowed African American policy analyst, came to treatment after months of feeling as if his body had never quite returned from a medical emergency that nearly killed him. Before the illness, he had been the kind of man who managed long reports, tracked legislation, and prided himself on steady judgment. During a winter afternoon at home, alone in the kitchen while reheating soup, he suddenly felt an intense pressure in his chest and a wave of breathlessness that forced him to sit down on the floor. He remembers the ambulance ride in fragments: the bright ceiling lights passing overhead, the smell of antiseptic, the abrupt voices of strangers, and the terrifying certainty that he might not see his late wife’s photograph on the mantel again. In the hospital, he was told that his condition was life-threatening, and he underwent treatment that left him exhausted, disoriented, and frightened by how quickly his own body had turned against him.

In the weeks afterward, Ezekiel found that the memories of that day were not stored as a settled story. At times he could recall the sequence of events almost mechanically, but it felt completely numb, as if it had happened to another man; at other times, the scene came back with such force that it felt as though the monitor alarms were sounding again in the present, not in the past. When that happened, he had to stop whatever he was doing and sit quietly until the wave passed. The memory was especially potent when he was at home, in the same kitchen where the episode had begun, or when he noticed a tightness in his chest after climbing stairs. Those moments pulled him back into the hospital room so vividly that he could hardly distinguish recollection from immediate danger.

As the physical crisis receded, Ezekiel’s fear did not. He became increasingly convinced that his body could not be trusted. He would catch himself checking his pulse, his breathing, and the feel of his chest when he walked from the bedroom to the kitchen, as if he were monitoring a machine that might fail without warning. He had come to believe that his body kept reacting as though it were still in danger, even when he was safe, and that belief sharpened his sense of threat. The more he noticed tension in his shoulders, a racing heart, or a flicker of dizziness, the more certain he became that another collapse could happen at any moment. Even inside his own home, where he had once felt most at ease, he felt on guard, as if he needed to stay ready for the next abrupt medical emergency.

That steady state of alertness made the memory of the illness easier to trigger and harder to shake. A twinge in his chest while bending to pick up files for work, or a moment of fatigue in the afternoon, could bring the hospital back with alarming vividness. Then the image would flood him: the stretcher, the masked staff, the helplessness of not knowing whether he would survive. At those times he was overwhelmed by emotion and had to stop speaking mid-sentence, sometimes in the middle of drafting policy notes at his office. His concentration suffered, and colleagues noticed that he was slower to respond in meetings and less willing to take on tasks that once came easily. The tense vigilance spread into his workday and into evenings at home, where he would sit stiffly in his armchair, listening to every sensation in his body.

The same episodes deepened his negative appraisals. Ezekiel told himself that he would never feel normal emotions again, only this strange flattened fear and numbness, and that his body had become an enemy that could turn on him without warning. He no longer trusted his own physical reactions; to him, every palpitating heartbeat seemed like proof that something dangerous was brewing beneath the surface. Those beliefs fed his watchfulness, and the watchfulness made each bodily sensation feel more ominous. Over time he began avoiding long walks near his apartment, hesitating before cooking alone, and staying close to a chair whenever he felt even slightly unsteady. He also withdrew from a few social dinners, embarrassed by how often he needed to sit down or excuse himself to “check something,” though he never fully put that fear into words.

By the time he sought help, Ezekiel was exhausted by the constant effort of bracing for the next sign of danger and by the shame of feeling unlike himself. He said he was most afraid that he would remain trapped in this state forever, unable to trust his body or feel fully alive again. What brought him in was the growing cost of living like this in his own home and at his desk, and the hope that he might learn how to face his body without waiting for it to betray him.
